info.description:
# AlphaProStudio — platform API

One collection for the whole platform, updated in the PR of every phase that adds or changes an endpoint (CLAUDE.md rule 13). `plan.md` is the technical reference; section numbers are cited per request.

## How this collection is organised

**Folders are CATEGORIES — the API groups of `plan.md` §6 — never build phases.**
A phase number says when something was built, which is history the repo already
keeps in `plan.md` and `.agent/sessions.md`. Someone opening this collection is
looking for *media* or *usage*, not for *F10*; and an endpoint that lands in one
phase and changes in three would otherwise have to live in the wrong folder
forever.

So a new endpoint goes in the folder its **URL prefix** belongs to, and a new
category is a new folder — not a new phase folder. The one folder that is not a
§6 group is **Test**, last: probes, diagnostics and fixture demos that are
not integration surface. Each category holds ONE request per
endpoint, asserting its success state; an endpoint with several body shapes is a
sub-folder named for the endpoint, one request per variation. Refusal behaviour
is documented in each request's description and pinned by the route/contract
suites in CI — it is not replayed here.

**Order is functional, not cosmetic.** `pnpm api:collection` runs this file top
to bottom and requests chain through variables (a source read reads the source a
create just made), so a producer must precede its consumers. That is why
**Knowledge (RAG)** sits ahead of **Capability runs**: the grounded runs need a
collection that already exists. Keep that property when you add requests.

## Setup — one command

```bash
pnpm api:env            # defaults to dev-hasan
```

That writes `docs/postman/dev-hasan.postman_environment.json` (git-ignored) with the stage's real base url, edge secret, app id, tenant, and HMAC key. In Postman: **Environments → Import →** pick that file **→** select **AlphaProStudio — dev-hasan** in the environment dropdown (top right). Then open any request and hit **Send** — signed requests build their own §6.1 signature in a pre-request script, so there is nothing to paste.

Re-run `pnpm api:env` after a secret rotation or a redeploy that changes the url.

Everything currently targets **dev-hasan**; staging and prod are stood up only once the app is ready. To run the whole collection headless instead:

```bash
pnpm api:collection     # newman, same values, also defaults to dev-hasan
```

**Never type a real secret into this file** — it is committed to git (CLAUDE.md rule 9). The variables below hold placeholders; the environment file supplies the real values.

## If a signed request suddenly returns 401 "signature mismatch"

Postman copies a collection on import and never re-reads the file, so after any pull that changes this collection you must **delete it in Postman and import again** — otherwise the pre-request scripts signing your requests are the previous version's. There is no session and no token expiry here; every request is signed on its own. The two time-bound checks name themselves: `timestamp outside the ±300 s window` (clock skew) and `replayed request` (nonce reused). `pnpm api:collection` reads the file directly and is never stale.

## Auth model (plan.md §12.1)

The platform never sees an end-user credential. Three app-scoped layers:

1. **Per-app HMAC** (§6.1) — all `/v1/*` service routes, including stream register. Exercised in **Service authentication**.
2. **Single-use stream ticket** (§2.5) — `GET /v1/stream/consume/:ticket` only. Exercised in **Streaming**.
3. **Per-app spend grant** (§10.3) — paid jobs. Exercised in **Media**.

On top of those, every deployed stage sits behind the **edge-secret ingress guard** (§5): CloudFront injects `x-aps-edge-secret` on staging/prod; on a dev Function URL you send it yourself.

## Errors

Every non-2xx response is `application/problem+json` using the fixed catalogue in §6.3 — `{ type, title, status, detail?, requestId }`. `type` is the only error vocabulary; apps map it to their own copy.

## Folders

| Folder | Endpoints | Auth |
|---|---|---|
| **Health & edge** | `GET /v1/health` · `GET /internal/stream-probe` | none — public (§6), behind the edge-secret guard on a deployed stage |
| **Service authentication** | `GET /v1/whoami` + the §6.1 refusal matrix | per-app HMAC |
| **Catalog** | `GET /v1/catalog` · `GET /v1/catalog/:alias` | per-app HMAC |
| **Knowledge (RAG)** | `/v1/rag/collections/*` · `/v1/rag/sources/*` · `POST /v1/rag/query` · `/v1/rag/migrations/*` | per-app HMAC |
| **Capability runs** | `POST /v1/run/:capability` · `GET /v1/runs/:id` | per-app HMAC |
| **Streaming** | `POST /v1/run/:capability` (`stream: true`) · `GET /v1/stream/consume/:ticket` | HMAC to register, single-use ticket to consume |
| **Media** | `/v1/media/jobs*` · `/v1/media/assets/*` · `POST /webhooks/media/:provider` | per-app HMAC + spend grant; webhooks are provider-signed |
| **Usage** | `GET /v1/usage` | per-app HMAC |

Every endpoint in `plan.md` §6 is present. When §6 gains a row, this table and
the matching folder gain one in the same PR.

item.name: Catalog
item.description:
The app's own view of what it may use (plan.md §6 — Catalog, §9.1).

A catalog row is a ROLE, not a vendor model, and an app sees it only through its own ALIAS. **No response here may contain a catalog model id, a provider, or a vendor model ref** — aliases resolve to vendor ids inside the engine and nowhere else. The tests assert exactly that, and they are the reason this folder exists as much as the endpoints are.

Since C8 the catalog also answers WHICH alias goes WHERE: every model lists the capabilities it may be named for, and `GET /v1/catalog/capabilities/:capability` reads the same derivation the other way round — including `selectable: false` for a capability that pins its models.

A model the app was not granted answers `403 model_not_enabled`, the same failure the engine raises when a run names an alias the app does not hold — so "this is not yours" is observable over HTTP.

The raw catalog reads (`GET /v1/catalog`, `GET /v1/catalog/:alias`) live in the Test folder (2026-08): apps integrate through capability discovery here; the raw list is platform diagnostics.

item.name: Knowledge (RAG)
item.description:
The knowledge subsystem (plan.md §6 — RAG, §10): collections and their sources, retrieval, and the embedding/chunk-profile migration lifecycle.

Scope is two-level like everything else: a collection is `scope: tenant` or `scope: app` (shared with every tenant of that app, never across apps), and filters are injected by the platform from verified context — a caller cannot pass a raw filter, because the interface has no parameter for one.

**Order matters across the collection.** Collections & sources creates the demo corpus the grounded capability runs below rely on. Retrieval and the migration lifecycle moved to the final Test folder (2026-08): they are platform-side surface, not app integration. `pnpm api:collection` still runs everything top to bottom.

Walk-through for using it by hand: `docs/USING-KNOWLEDGE-POSTMAN.md`.

item.name: Collections & sources
item.description:
Creating a corpus and putting documents in it (plan.md §6, §10.1).

A collection pins one embedding model and one chunk profile; sources arrive by push, by SSRF-safe URL fetch, or by presigned upload, and flow `Uploading → Processing → Ready | Failed(reason)` with `ingestion.status` callbacks along the way. Content-hash dedupe makes re-ingestion a no-op, and deleting a source removes its vectors before the call returns.

The cross-tenant and cross-app reads here return `404`, not `403`: a source that is not yours does not exist as far as you are concerned.

Adds a source to the collection (plan.md §10.1). `push` sends text you already have; `url` has the platform fetch it under the §12.2 SSRF rules (http/https only — the schema itself refuses `file://`).

**202, not 200:** ingestion is asynchronous. The source comes back `Processing`; extraction, chunking and embedding happen on `q-ingest` and `q-embed`, and the app learns the outcome from the `ingestion.status` callback or by polling the source.

**Auth:** per-app HMAC. The bytes are stored under `knowledge/<app>/<tenant>/<source>/` — the two-level scope is in the object key itself (§5).

**202 response:**
```json
{ "sourceId": "src_…", "collectionId": "col_…", "kind": "push",
  "status": "Processing", "chunkCount": 0, "deduped": false }
```

item.description:
The two-call ticket flow (plan.md §2.5, §6.2). **No end-user token ever reaches the platform.**

item.name: Migrations
item.description:
Moving a collection to a different embedding model or chunk profile with no downtime (plan.md §6, §10.4).

`created → backfilling → dual_write → evaluating → flipped | rolled_back → gc_done`. The whole machine runs on `q-migrate`, one bounded step per message, so a corpus of any size migrates and a step that dies replays from its stored cursor. **The alias flips only if the new index meets the gate** — completeness (one vector per chunk) and retrieval quality (both indexes scored on the same questions, each with its own embedding model, against absolutes *and* a regression bound).

One live migration per collection, enforced by a partial-unique index — which is why a second `migrate` answers `400`. Exactly one target per request, because a migration changing both model and profile would have no rollback pointer.

`POST /webhooks/media/:provider` (§6) is PUBLIC — no HMAC, no ticket. The PROVIDER's own signature is the authorization: fal signs ED25519 over its own canonical string, Replicate uses standard-webhooks HMAC, and Runware — which publishes no scheme at all — is authenticated by a platform-minted per-job token in the callback url.

Losing that index degrades to the §9.3 sweeper — the same path a genuinely lost webhook takes.
